doc.title: Al Vollmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

chapter: Founding the Harlem Blues and Jazz Band
title: Fixing Punch Miller's tooth and testing musicians on records
summary: He made a partial denture so Punch Miller could hit the high D, then played him records; Miller denied one he wasn't on, shaping Vollmer's view that musicians know their own work.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

I helped Louie Nelson, I helped Andrew Morgan. Those were the New Orleans guys. And once Punch Miller was staying at Bill Bissonnette’s house in Bridgeport, Connecticut, which is about an hour, little more than an hour away from me. And he calls me up in the morning and he says, “We’re going to record ‘West End Blues’ and Punch can’t hit the high D because something’s going on with his teeth, can you take a look?” So he brought him down and I looked and I saw that he was missing an upper molar, he had a partial denture, and I figured the air was going out there. And luckily I had a wonderful, wonderful lab guy. I took impressions and Bill Bissonnette went back up to Connecticut. Punch stayed with me, and I remember Dot serving him lunch, and at that point I’d taken impressions and they were now at the lab and back it came with the tooth where it was necessary for it to be. And Bill Bissonnette came back and picked him up and they recorded and he hit the high D. And I said, “Okay, Bill, now you’re going to do something for me. I know you and your wife go to work in the morning. I want to come up there — and Punch is staying at your house — I want to have Punch completely to myself, and I want to play him the records and see, because there are dubious things about where he might be. The record I really wanted to play for him, which I did, was Early on one Christmas morn/Jesus Christ the king was born/By the Cotton Top Mountain — something or other. I had it on a 78. And there’s a brilliant trumpet there that takes two choruses and it’s kind of tricky, uh, execution. Kind of tricky ex — and I thought it was Punch. I put the record on and Punch said, “Oh no.” Punch said, “Who’s that, that’s not me” he said, “that’s not my style.” And so then I played him the Tiny Parhams and sure enough he identified himself where we know he is. And then I put on the same record over again and I said, “Punch, here’s another record.” He denied it again. And it’s listed — it was listed in the books at that time, the Cotton Top Mountain Singers or something. And so he denied himself twice, and I tried to trick him. But, so my experience with playing records for the musicians, they know their own work, they won’t claim anything they didn’t do, and you need to double check what they might say about who else is on the record. That was my philosophy.
